extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and critics of poetry and literary theory; readers of Coleridge's Biographia Literaria
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and analysis of the principles that govern poetic imagination and fancy (including the law of association) and guidance on how to present a coherent poetic theory. Includes historical tracing of psychological and philosophical doctrines that inform poetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the influences of fancy and imagination as manifested in poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Wordsworth's purpose to consider the influences of fancy and imagination as they are manifested in poetry, and from the different effects to conclude their diversity in kind; the author's object is to investigate the seminal principle, and then from the kind to deduce the degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish diversity in kind (fancy vs imagination) and then measure degree; Wordsworth 'draws a masterly sketch of the branches with their poetic fruitage' while the author aims to add the trunk and roots visible to common consciousness. Use analogy (branches/trunk/roots) to orient analysis from effects to underlying principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present an intelligible statement of poetic creed deductively
rubrics_metrics.description: Present an intelligible statement of my poetic creed — not as my opinions, which weigh for nothing, but as deductions from established premises conveyed in such a form as is calculated either to effect a fundamental conviction, or to receive a fundamental confutation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not offer mere personal opinion; base claims on established premises and present them so they can either convince or be refuted. Be prepared to draw on readers' attention and accept that some will choose not to engage. Aim for form that invites serious scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspicuity, port and dignity of language; anticipate obscurity complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: Hooker is admired for perspicuity as well as for the port and dignity of his language; though he wrote for learned men, he anticipated and guarded against 'complaints of obscurity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when writing for learned audiences or on deep subjects, strive for clarity and graceful expression; expect and preempt objections about obscurity. Drawing on the reader's attention may be necessary where material is novel or intricate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Association (contemporaneity of impressions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of association as established in the contemporaneity of the original impressions: contemporaneous impressions, whether images or sensations, recall each other mechanically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat association as a fundamental psychological principle underlying thought, language, and imagination. Trace its formulations historically (Aristotle, Vives, Descartes, Hobbes, Hartley, Hume) and use it to explain how ideas become linked and how one impression can recall others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate other causes of association to Time
rubrics_metrics.description: Vives (and others) subordinate all other exciting causes of association to Time: 'to time, therefore, he subordinates all the other exciting causes of association... the soul proceeds a causa ad effectum, ab hoc ad instrumentum, a parte ad totum...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain associative linkage primarily by temporal relations (contemporaneity or sequence). Use historical or mnemonic examples (e.g., Scipio→Antiochus via victories in Asia) to illustrate long leaps of association when items were components of multiple total impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association explains speech and habit
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes' account that repeated impingement of the senses produces motions that become habitual and underlie speech: 'custom hath so great a power, that the mind suggesteth only the first word; the rest follow habitually.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the mechanism of habitual, mechanically-linked impressions to explain discursions of mind, the onset of speech, and automaticity in expression. Relate repeated sensory/motor patterns to linguistic and mental habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground historical or priority claims on documentary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When asserting historical precedence or the origination of doctrines (e.g., whether Hobbes discovered the law of association), accuracy should be tested 'by documents rather than reasoning.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support claims about who discovered or first formulated an idea with primary sources and documentary evidence. Avoid asserting priority on the basis of inference alone; check antecedent writings (Aristotle, Vives, Descartes, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define philosophical terms precisely and avoid vague uses (e.g., 'idea')
rubrics_metrics.description: The vague use of the word 'idea' has caused much error and confusion; the term has different senses in Plato, Locke, Hume, and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly define key terms (idea, impression, image, imagination, fancy) as used in your argument. Discuss differing historical uses and adopt precise definitions to prevent equivocation and conceptual confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use physiological/empirical explanations carefully but critically
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes and others attempt to explain association by material/mechanical causes (motions of organs, nervous fluids); Hobbes introduces the law of association as an admitted fact solved by causes 'purely physiological.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When invoking physiological or mechanistic accounts of mental phenomena, acknowledge limits and potential incompatibilities with other metaphysical commitments (e.g., pure materialism vs idealism). Use empirical illustrations but be cautious about overextending physiological metaphors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ concrete illustrative examples from perception and experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors use examples (operation of natural objects on the mind; Descartes' anecdote of the amputated child's phantom pains) to illustrate associative principles and difficulties in attributing place to inward pains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative anecdotes and empirical instances are effective for clarifying abstract doctrines; select vivid, relevant examples (natural phenomena, case stories) to show how associative laws operate in perception, memory, and language.
